lines.text: A landlocked heart of South America where most people still speak Guarani, a country nearly destroyed by war and rebuilt. This is the story of Paraguay.
In 1537 Spanish explorers founded Asuncion on the Paraguay River, one of the oldest cities in South America.
In the forests to the south, Jesuit priests gathered the Guarani into missions, until the order was expelled in 1767. Their stone ruins still stand.
In 1766 Jose Gaspar Rodriguez de Francia was born, the dictator who would seal his country off from the world.
In 1811 Paraguay broke free from Spain, and soon Francia ruled it alone for a quarter of a century.
In 1826 Francisco Solano Lopez was born, the president who would lead his country into catastrophe.
In 1864 Paraguay went to war with Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay together. By the end in 1870, it had lost land and most of its men.
In 1912 Alfredo Stroessner was born, the general who would rule Paraguay for thirty-five years.
Five years later came Augusto Roa Bastos, whose novel I the Supreme looked hard at the country's dictators.
In 1932 Paraguay and Bolivia went to war over the dry Chaco. Three years later, Paraguay won.
Under Stroessner, Paraguay and Brazil began the giant Itaipu Dam on the Parana River, which opened in 1984.
In 1978 Santiago Pena was born, who became president in 2023.
From Jesuit missions to one of the world's great dams, Paraguay has risen again and again.
